title: Extending Debye-Hückel Theory to Higher Concentrations
lead: Debye–Hückel theory rests on simplifying assumptions about ions and solvent that stop holding as solutions get more concentrated. Empirical extensions add terms that keep its low-concentration behavior and fit measurements at higher ionic strength.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page, which is adapted from Wikipedia under CC BY-SA 4.0; Figure 25.7.1's original is by PChemiker (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the points in its redrawing are read off Figure 25.6.2 (Petergans, public domain).
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; the one exercise is new and AI-written, with an AI solution, and its answers were checked by computation.

figures.original_caption: Semi-log plot of activity coefficients calculated using the Davies equation. (CC BY-SA 4.0; PChemiker via [Wikipedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ActivityCoefficientsDaviesEquation_lin.png))

exercises.source_id: For 1:1 electrolytes the difference between measured values and those calculated with this equation
exercises.prompt: Calculate the mean activity coefficient of 0.10 mol/L NaCl at 25 °C (a) by the limiting law $\log γ_\pm = -A|z_+z_-|\sqrt{I}$, (b) by the extended Debye–Hückel equation with $a = 3$ Å, using $A = 0.5085$ and $B = 0.3281$, and (c) by the Davies equation. Which would you trust at this concentration, and why?

parts.hint: For NaCl the ionic strength equals the concentration and $|z_+z_-| = 1$.

answer.solution:
For NaCl, $I = 0.10$ mol/L and $\sqrt{I} = 0.316$.

(a) $\log γ_\pm = -(0.5085)(0.316) = -0.161$, so $γ_\pm = 0.690$.

(b) The denominator is $1 + (0.3281)(3)(0.316) = 1.311$, so $\log γ_\pm = -0.161/1.311 = -0.123$ and $γ_\pm = 0.754$.

(c) $-\log f_\pm = 0.5\left(\dfrac{0.316}{1.316} - 0.030\right) = 0.105$, so $f_\pm = 0.785$.

The limiting law holds only below about $10^{-3}$ mol/L, a hundred times more dilute, and it is far too low here. The Davies equation is fitted to data and is good to about 2% for 1:1 electrolytes at 0.1 M, so it is the one to trust; the extended equation comes closer than the limiting law because it allows for the size of the ions.

footnotes.html: The ionic strength is $I$, the symbol in the equation, not $\mu$.
Both axes of the plot are linear: it shows the activity coefficient $f$ itself against $I$, not on a logarithmic scale.
